who: Basil was bishop of Caesarea, in today's Turkey, in the 300s. He left a speaker's career to become a monk. His Rules shaped Orthodox monastic life. As a priest he fed the hungry in a famine. As bishop he built a house for the sick and stood up to an emperor. He is one of the Cappadocian Fathers.

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 329 or 330, at Caesarea in Cappadocia, today **Kayseri in Turkey**. Some older writers said Neocaesarea in Pontus. His family had lands in both.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: On the family estate by the river Iris, in Pontus. Then at school in Caesarea, Constantinople and **Athens**. His father, also Basil, taught rhetoric. His grandmother Macrina and his father taught him the faith.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: The eldest son of ten children. His sister **Macrina**, his brothers **Gregory of Nyssa** and **Peter of Sebaste**, his mother and his grandmother are all counted saints.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **1 January 379**, at Caesarea, worn out by illness and a hard life. He was about 49.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At Caesarea, in “the tomb of his fathers”. The crowd at his funeral was so great that many people were crushed to death.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Basil of Caesarea**. **Basil the Great**, already in his brother's words: “the great Basil”. To the Orthodox, one of the **Three Holy Hierarchs**, with Gregory the Theologian and John Chrysostom. **Vasily Veliky**, in Russian.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too. A **Doctor of the Church** to Catholics.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In icons, a thin bishop with a long, dark, pointed beard, in white vestments marked with crosses, holding a book or a scroll. Gregory says people even copied “his paleness, his beard, his gait”.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: About 325 letters that are really his. **On the Holy Spirit**. Nine sermons on the six days of creation, the **Hexaemeron**. Books against Eunomius. The **Rules** for monks, and many sermons. An **Address to Young Men**, on reading Greek literature.

portrait.alt: Saint Basil, an old bishop with a long grey beard and a white mitre, sits with a quill and an open book while monks and bishops around him write, and the dove of the Holy Spirit flies above
portrait.credit: Saint Basil Dictating His Doctrine, Francisco de Herrera the Elder, about 1639. Musée du Louvre, Paris. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Francisco de Herrera the Elder
portrait.caption: A Spanish painting of about 1639, by Francisco de Herrera the Elder. Basil dictates his teaching, monks and bishops write it down, and the dove of the Holy Spirit flies above. Louvre, Paris. Public domain.

typeNote: The Herald is sure of itself, and at its best with something to do. The test names him as a young man, fresh from university and proud of his speaking, before his sister Macrina turned him round.

west.text: **Catholic** memorial, shared with his friend Gregory Nazianzen. Also the **Church of England**, with Gregory, a Lesser Festival.
Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod**, with Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa.
**Episcopal Church**. Lutherans in the **ELCA**, with the two Gregorys and Macrina. Also the **1916 Roman Martyrology**, which kept his feast on this day.

east.text: **Greek** churches and the **OCA**. The day he died.
**Russian Church**. This is 1 January on the old calendar.
The **Three Holy Hierarchs**, in **Greek** churches and the **OCA**. The OCA says that in the eleventh century people in Constantinople argued over which of the three was the greatest.
**Russian Church**, the Three Holy Hierarchs. This is 30 January on the old calendar.

feasts.note: Why so many dates? The East keeps 1 January, the day he died. The old Western calendars kept 14 June, by tradition the day he was made bishop. Today's Catholic calendar and the Church of England keep him on 2 January, beside his friend Gregory. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later, so 1 January falls on 14 January.

traits.title: unafraid of power
traits.text: The emperor's prefect threatened him with “Confiscation, banishment, torture, death.” Basil said none of them could touch him. He owned nothing but rags and a few books, and every land was God's. The prefect said no one had ever spoken to him like that. Basil answered, “Why, perhaps, you have not met with a Bishop.”

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 49 and 50

traits.title: taken for proud
traits.text: Some called him proud. Gregory answered that “what they term pride is, I fancy, the firmness and steadfastness and stability of his character.” He was sparing with praise: “His very smile often amounted to praise, his silence to rebuke.” Yet in company, Gregory asks, “Who was more kindly in his stories, more refined in his wit, more tender in his rebukes?”

traits.title: a sharp pen
traits.text: His letters could bite. His brother Gregory forged a letter from their uncle, a bishop, and brought it to him. A second came by Gregory's servant, and it was not the bishop's either. When a third came, Basil wrote to his brother, “who ever falls a third time into the same nets?” On courting the bishops of the West for help, he wrote, “Really lofty souls, when they are courted, get haughtier than ever.”

traits.title: hard on himself
traits.text: He lived on bread and salt, with one coat, a worn cloak and a bed on the bare ground. When a judge threatened him with blows, he offered to be torn with combs. It would cure his liver, he said, “which, as you see, is wearing me away.” Gregory calls him “the poorest and most needy man whom I have known”.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 36, 57 and 61

said.lede: Most of his story comes from his best friend, Gregory of Nazianzus, who gave the speech at his funeral. His brother Gregory of Nyssa and his own letters add more.

quotes.q: We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.
quotes.who: Gregory of Nazianzus, on their student days at Athens

quotes.q: …glorify the Lord Who has given such a bishop to Cappadocia as any district must pray to have.
quotes.who: Athanasius of Alexandria, in 372, when monks at Caesarea were attacking Basil

quotes.q: Basil, our common father and teacher
quotes.who: Gregory of Nyssa, his younger brother

cite.text: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Making of Man, dedication

moments.title: Friends at Athens
moments.text: At Athens he was together again with his friend Gregory, from Nazianzus. New students there were mocked, then marched to the baths in a noisy hazing. Gregory talked the others out of it, so Basil “was the only one to escape the general rule”. The two knew only two roads: one to church and one to their teachers. Parties and theatres they left to others.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 16 to 21

moments.title: The proud young speaker
moments.text: He came home a star speaker. His brother says he was “puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory”, and looked down on the leading men of the town. Their older sister Macrina took him in hand. He gave up his career and all his property. He later wrote that he woke as if from a deep sleep, and wept over his life. Then he went to see the monks of Egypt, Palestine, Syria and Mesopotamia.

cite.text: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina; Basil, Letter 223, chapter 2

moments.title: A monk in Pontus
moments.text: He settled on the family lands in Pontus and gathered monks around him. He wrote to Gregory, “I have abandoned my life in town, as one sure to lead to countless ills; but I have not yet been able to get quit of myself.” In time he joined the hermit's life to life in community. Gregory says he built hermits' cells close to the shared houses, so that the life of prayer and the active life would not be cut off from each other.

cite.text: Basil, Letter 2, chapter 1; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapter 62

moments.title: The famine
moments.text: A famine struck, the worst anyone remembered. Grain dealers held back their stores to drive prices up. Basil, still a priest, preached until the rich opened their barns. Then he gathered the hungry of every age and set out “basins of soup”. With his own servants he waited on them himself, as Christ washed His disciples' feet. Gregory calls him a second Joseph.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 34 to 36

moments.title: The emperor in church
moments.text: The emperor Valens favoured the Arians, and his prefect had failed to frighten Basil. “We have been worsted, Sire, by the prelate of this Church,” the prefect reported. On the feast of the Epiphany, Valens came to Basil's church himself. The thunder of the psalms, the sea of people, and Basil standing still “as if, so to say, he had been a statue” overwhelmed him. He staggered, and someone had to reach out a hand to steady him.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 51 and 52; Theodoret, Church History, Book 4, chapter 16

moments.title: The new city
moments.text: Just outside Caesarea he built what Gregory calls the new city. It had a church, lodging for travellers, and doctors for the sick. Lepers, driven out of their towns, were cared for there. Basil, a nobleman, “saluted them as brethren” and kissed them. Theodoret says the emperor himself gave land for the poor in Basil's care.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 63 and 64; Basil, Letter 94; Theodoret, Church History, Book 4, chapter 16

moments.title: A bishopric for his best friend
moments.text: The province was split in two. Anthimus, bishop of the new capital, Tyana, claimed the churches of the new half for himself. To hold his ground, Basil made new bishops. He made Gregory bishop of Sasima, a small village. Gregory wrote to him, “Give me before all things quiet.” Years later, in his funeral speech, he still called it “a cause of pain which even time has not obliterated.”

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 58 and 59; Letter 48; Jackson, Prolegomena

moments.title: A book about the Spirit
moments.text: Praying with his people, he gave glory to the Father “with the Son together with the Holy Ghost”. Some who were there attacked him for it. His friend Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, asked him to explain. The answer was On the Holy Spirit. It argues that the Spirit shares the glory of the Father and the Son.

miracles.lede: Gregory says Basil could not “rain bread from heaven by prayer”, as Moses did in the wilderness. But he tells of healings, and of wonders when Basil was made bishop and when he died.

more.title: The emperor's son
more.text: The order to exile Basil was signed, and his carriage stood ready. That night the emperor's small son fell ill with a fever. The doctors could do nothing, and Valens threw himself on the ground in grief. Too ashamed to ask himself, he sent friends to fetch Basil. When Basil came, the fever eased at once. But Valens called in Arian clergy as well, and the boy died. Gregory says he would have lived, had Valens not “blended salt water with the fresh”. He adds, “This indeed was the conviction of those who were present at the time, and shared in the distress.”
more.quote: On his arrival, without the delay or reluctance which any one else might have shown, at once the disease relaxed, and the father cherished better hopes

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapter 54; Theodoret, Church History, Book 4, chapter 16; Sozomen, Church History, Book 6, chapter 16

more.title: The prefect
more.text: Then Modestus, the prefect who had threatened Basil, fell ill in his turn. In tears he sent for Basil and begged him. He got well, and afterwards he never stopped telling people what Basil could do.
more.quote: I own that you were in the right; only save me!

more.title: The old bishop in the litter
more.text: When Basil was chosen bishop, Gregory's father, the aged bishop of Nazianzus, set out to vote for him and help consecrate him. He was so ill that he was carried in a litter. He went home, says his son, “in the freshness and strength of youth, with head erect”.
more.quote: he was placed in his litter, as a corpse is laid in its tomb

more.title: Strength on his deathbed
more.text: He was almost dead and barely breathing. Yet he grew stronger for his last words, long enough to ordain the best of his disciples as priests. Gregory calls it “a wonder in no wise inferior to those mentioned before”.
more.quote: he grew stronger in his last words, so as to depart with the utterances of religion

more.title: Three broken pens
more.text: Later, says Theodoret, Valens again signed an order to exile Basil. The pen broke. A second pen broke, and a third. His hand shook, and he tore the order up with both hands.
more.quote: for the pen broke, and when the same thing happened to the second and to the third pen, and he still strove to sign that wicked edict, his hand shook

doubt.title: The sources disagree
doubt.text: Socrates, another church historian, tells the story of the emperor's son with no healing at all. In his version Basil sets terms, and Valens refuses them. Basil says, “God's will concerning the child will be done then,” and “the child, however, died shortly after.” Sozomen says the boy began to rally when Basil came. Of the rest he says only that “many maintain that his recovery would have been complete”. Even Gregory begins the prefect's story with “is said to have”.

words.note: Basil wrote a great deal that survives. These are his own words, in Blomfield Jackson's translation of 1895 and W. K. Lowther Clarke's of 1925.

feature.q: Whose feet then wilt thou wash? Whom wilt thou care for? In comparison with whom wilt thou be last if thou livest by thyself?
feature.ctx: From his Rules, arguing that monks should live together. Just before, he recalls that Christ washed the disciples' feet Himself. As a young monk he had written that “solitude is of the greatest use”. This is his later view.

quotes.q: Death is my benefactor, for it will send me the sooner to God, for Whom I live, and exist, and have all but died, and to Whom I have long been hastening.
quotes.who: To the prefect, who had threatened him with death. As Gregory of Nazianzus reports it.

quotes.q: Much time had I spent in vanity, and had wasted nearly all my youth in the vain labour which I underwent in acquiring the wisdom made foolish by God. Then once upon a time, like a man roused from deep sleep, I turned my eyes to the marvellous light of the truth of the Gospel.
quotes.who: Looking back on his turn to Christ, almost twenty years later.

quotes.q: We have not lost the lad; we have restored him to the Lender. His life is not destroyed; it is changed for the better.
quotes.who: To his friend Nectarius, whose son, the heir of the house, had died as a young man.

quotes.q: I want creation to penetrate you with so much admiration that everywhere, wherever you may be, the least plant may bring to you the clear remembrance of the Creator.
quotes.who: To his people, preaching on the third day of creation.

quotes.q: For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense.
quotes.who: Against those who turned everything in Genesis into symbols. In the same sermon he leaves the shape of the earth alone, because Moses “is silent as to shapes”.

quotes.q: But to whom do we do any harm by building a place of entertainment for strangers, both for those who are on a journey and for those who require medical treatment on account of sickness?
quotes.who: To the governor, who had heard complaints about his building outside Caesarea.

quotes.q: But for prayer and psalmody, as for many other things, every time is suitable; so that we praise God with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs while we move our hands in work.
quotes.who: To monks who skipped work to pray.

quotes.q: Harshness is ever to be put aside, even in censuring.
quotes.who: Advice to his friend Gregory, on how to speak to others.

stood.lede: Each line is Basil's own. Many come from his Rules, which he wrote for monks, not for everyone. Two are our own translations from his Greek sermons, because we found no public-domain English of them.

anger.work: Homily against Anger, as Blomfield Jackson quotes it

tears.work: Letter 269, to the wife of Arinthaeus the general

extras.title: The hard parts
extras.lede: Some of what he wrote is hard to read today. Here it is plainly, in his own words and his friends'.

items.title: Slavery
items.text: He accepted slavery. Runaway slaves who came to his monasteries were to be “admonished and made better, and then restored” to their masters, as Paul sent Onesimus back to Philemon. If a master ordered a slave to sin, the monks were to prepare the slave to suffer for obeying God, or else take on the troubles that keeping him might bring.

items.title: Third marriages
items.text: Passing on older church rules, he wrote that a third marriage was “no longer described as marriage at all, but as polygamy; nay rather as limited fornication.” Such people were kept from communion for years. Yet they “ought not to be altogether prohibited from the privileges of the Church”.

items.title: Laughter
items.text: Writing for monks, he said “there is never a time of laughter for the believer”, since so many around are dead in sin. In another Rule he allows “a cheerful smile”, but not loud laughter that shakes the body. His friend Gregory remembered his refined wit.

cite.text: The Shorter Rules, Rule 31; The Longer Rules, Rule 17

items.title: Holding back on the Spirit
items.text: In public he would not say the plain words “the Spirit is God”. The Arians were waiting for them, as a reason to exile him and seize his church. Monks attacked him for it. Athanasius defended him. Gregory calls it his “economy”. He says Basil often preached this truth in public when he could, and confessed it gladly in private.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 68 and 69; Athanasius, Letter 63

items.title: Soldiers who kill
items.text: He wrote that the Fathers before him did not count killing in war as murder. But he added a counsel of his own.
items.quote: Perhaps, however, it is well to counsel that those whose hands are not clean only abstain from communion for three years.

myths.claim: He wrote the well-loved prayer for the animals, “our brothers”, that goes round under his name.
myths.truth: Not his. It comes from Walter Rauschenbusch's Prayers of the Social Awakening, printed in Boston in 1910. His prayer asks God to “enlarge within us the sense of fellowship with all the living things, our little brothers”. The popular version rewords it.

cite.text: Rauschenbusch, Prayers of the Social Awakening, For This World

myths.claim: His famous line about the bread you store up, the coat hanging in your closet, and the money in your vaults.
myths.truth: His in substance, from his sermon on the rich fool who planned bigger barns. But that wording is a loose modern paraphrase. In the Greek the cloak is kept in storerooms, not hanging in a closet, and there are no vaults. It does have the shoes rotting away with you, and the silver you have buried.

cite.text: Homily on *I will pull down my barns*, the Greek text

myths.claim: He hid gold coins in a loaf and gave them back to the people of Caesarea. That is where the Vasilopita comes from, the New Year cake with a coin inside.
myths.truth: Greek Orthodox parishes tell it as a pious story. It is not in Gregory's funeral speech, nor in the three church historians who tell his story. The real Basil did write to officials about taxes. He even asked Modestus, the prefect who had threatened him, to leave his clergy out of a new census, as the old one had.

cite.text: St Andrew Greek Orthodox Church, 2015; Basil, Letter 104, to Modestus

myths.claim: In a vision he saw the martyr Mercurius sent to kill the emperor Julian. The hermit Ephrem saw him as a pillar of fire.
myths.truth: These come from a Life said to be by his friend Amphilochius. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls it “a forgery of about the ninth century”. The medieval Golden Legend spread its stories, and even gets the year of his death wrong. Julian died in 363, before Basil was a bishop.

myths.claim: He wrote the Divine Liturgy of St Basil.
myths.truth: It bears his name, and the OCA says he composed it. The Catholic Encyclopedia is less sure. The Liturgy goes back at least to the sixth century, it says, but “its connexion with Basil has been a matter of critical discussion”.

circle.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
circle.text: His best friend, from their student days at Athens. They fell out when Basil made him bishop of Sasima. Gregory still gave the great speech at his funeral.

circle.name: Macrina the Younger
circle.text: His older sister, the eldest of the ten children. When he came home proud of his speaking, she drew him to the monk's life, working with his hands.

cite.text: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina

circle.name: Gregory of Nyssa
circle.text: His younger brother. Basil made him bishop of Nyssa in 372. After Basil died, Gregory finished his sermons on the days of creation.

cite.text: Jackson, Prolegomena; Socrates, Church History, Book 4, chapter 26

circle.name: Peter of Sebaste
circle.text: His youngest brother. Basil ordained him priest. Peter later became bishop of Sebaste.

cite.text: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina; Jackson, Prolegomena

circle.name: Macrina the Elder
circle.text: His grandmother. The 1916 Roman Martyrology says she was a disciple of Gregory the Wonderworker, and that she brought Basil up in the Christian faith.

circle.name: Emmelia and Basil the Elder
circle.text: His parents. His father, also Basil, was a lawyer and a teacher of rhetoric. His mother Emmelia was the daughter of a martyr.

circle.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
circle.text: The old defender of the Council of Nicaea. When monks at Caesarea attacked Basil, Athanasius wrote that he was “a glory to the Church”, and that they should obey him.

circle.name: Eustathius of Sebasteia
circle.text: An older monk he admired in his early years. Later they fell out, in part over the Holy Spirit. In 375, after three years of silence, Basil answered him in writing.

circle.name: Valens and Modestus
circle.text: The emperor and his prefect, who favoured the Arians and tried to bend Basil with threats. Both came to respect him. Later Basil wrote to Modestus asking favours for his clergy.

circle.name: Anthimus of Tyana
circle.text: Bishop of Tyana. When Cappadocia was split in two, he claimed the churches of the new half for himself. Once he blocked Basil's road and seized his mules.

cite.text: Oration 43, chapter 58; Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 48

death.big: He died at Caesarea on 1 January 379, about 49 years old, worn out by illness and a hard life.
paras: The whole city crowded round him as he lay dying. People wished they could give him some of their own years.
At his funeral “tens of thousands of every race and age” came, Jews and pagans among them. The crush was so great that many people died. He was laid in the tomb of his fathers.
Gregory was not there. He was gravely ill himself, and wrote to Basil's brother that he could not “kiss that holy dust”.

later.title: A later story
later.text: The medieval Golden Legend, following the forged Life, tells of a Jewish doctor named Joseph. Joseph told Basil, “This day shalt thou die when the sun shall go down in the west.” Basil lived until noon the next day, and baptised Joseph with his own hands.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Basil

items.q: Into Thy Hands I commend my spirit.
items.ctx: The words of Christ on the cross, from Luke 23:46.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too.

paras: He was never condemned. The Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran calendars all keep his day. The old Roman Martyrology kept his feast on the day he was made bishop:

quotes.q: …the consecration of St. Basil, bishop and doctor of the Church, who was eminent for learning and wisdom in the time of the emperor Valens. Being adorned with every virtue, he was a great light in the Church, and defended her with admirable constancy against the Arians and Macedonians.
quotes.who: The Roman Martyrology, 1916 edition, for 14 June

kin.text: When God asked, “Whom shall I send?”, he did not wait to be asked twice: “Here am I. Send me!”

kin.name: Peter
kin.text: “Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will,” he said. That same night he denied Christ three times. Then he wept, came back, and led the Church.

tidbits.text: During the persecution his father's family hid in the forests of Pontus for about seven years. When they longed for meat, says Gregory of Nazianzus, stags came down from the hills to be caught.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, chapters 5 to 8

tidbits.text: He preached his nine sermons on creation in Lent, morning and evening. Seeing working men crowd round him, he cut one short so as not to keep them from their work.
His 313 Shorter Rules seem to have been taken down in shorthand at an all-night meeting with the heads of monasteries, says their translator. Each heading is a question someone actually asked.

cite.text: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil, introduction

tidbits.text: Benedict's Rule for monks ends by pointing its readers on to older guides. One is the Rule of Basil, whom it calls our holy Father.
